s: Welcome back to Word Kitchen, everyone.
Today's episode is all about money and shopping, two things everyone has strong feelings about.
Lena, how would you describe your relationship with money in one sentence?
I shop when I'm happy or stressed, and I almost never check my balance first.
I'm the most frugal person in my friend group.
I plan my spending like a military operation.
You once spent three weeks researching a toaster.
And it's the best toaster I've ever owned.
It's about making sure every dollar works hard.
Meanwhile I have the opposite problem.
I tend to squander money on things I barely use.
Last spring I squandered a huge chunk of my savings on kitchen gadgets.
A bread maker, a juicer, a fancy espresso machine.
I used each of them twice.
Now they just sit there, judging me.
The trick is the forty-eight-hour rule.
If you still want it after forty-eight hours, then consider it.
I can't wait forty-eight minutes when there's a sale involved.
That's exactly when you need the rule most.
Sale signs are designed to short-circuit your brain.
And you know what else I never do?
I just pay whatever the tag says, even at flea markets.
That's leaving money on the table.
Sellers at markets expect you to haggle.
The first price is an opening offer, not a final answer.
My grandmother was a master of it.
She could haggle a street vendor down to half price and they'd both walk away smiling.
It takes confidence and humor, and honestly it's respectful.
You're engaging with the seller as a person.
I grew up in a pretty affluent suburb where nobody ever discussed prices.
Talking about money was considered terribly rude.
In affluent neighborhoods, the shops know customers won't question prices.
So they charge whatever they like.
The boutiques near my parents add an enormous markup to everything.
A simple cotton shirt sells for two hundred dollars, and most of that is pure profit.
That markup pays for the fancy lighting, the perfume they spray in the store, the shopping bags with ribbon handles.
And the rent on that street is astronomical, so the markup has to cover that too.
This is why I love outlet malls.
Same brands, far smaller markup, and nobody judges you for hunting bargains.
I went to an outlet last month and felt like a genius.
I bought a winter coat for a third of the downtown price.
A careful shopper compares prices, waits for sales, and never pays the first price they see.
She furnishes her whole apartment secondhand and it looks like a design magazine.
Thrifty people are often the most creative.
When you can't just throw money at a problem, you invent solutions.
But then there's my cousin's wedding last summer.
The most lavish event I've ever attended.
Three hundred guests, a string quartet, fireworks over the lake.
That sounds beautiful and terrifyingly expensive.
All that lavish spending, and half the guests left before dessert.
They could have invited eighty people and saved a fortune.
There's nothing wrong with celebrating, but lavish for the sake of lavish rarely makes anyone happier.
Some of my favorite evenings have been the simplest.
Takeout with friends costs almost nothing and I remember every one.
Now, have you ever received an unexpected sum of money?
A bonus, a refund, anything like that?
Two years ago my company gave everyone a surprise bonus.
It felt like a total windfall.
And what did you do with this windfall?
I booked a beach vacation within a week.
I treated that windfall like free money.
Money you didn't expect feels less real, so you spend it faster.
Then my car needed new brakes, and I wished I'd saved at least half of the windfall.
Financial planners say the same thing every time.
Save half of any unexpected money before you even think about spending it.
Speaking of spending, restaurant prices have become absolutely exorbitant lately, don't you think?
I paid thirty-eight dollars for a salad last week.
At some point expensive doesn't describe it anymore.
When the bill arrives and you laugh out loud, that's exorbitant.
I've started cooking much more at home.
When prices get that exorbitant, restaurants lose me as a customer.
My instincts kick in hard at those moments.
I'd rather make a great meal at home than overpay for a mediocre one.
You know what quietly drains my account?
Each one is small, but together they're a flood.
Oh, I did an audit last month and found eleven active subscriptions.
I was paying for three music services at the same time.
I put every renewal date in my calendar now.
I canceled seven of them in one evening and instantly felt richer.
It was the easiest money I've ever saved.
And online shopping is the other trap.
One-click buying removes every moment of reflection.
There's no walk to the register, no line, no pause.
I see an ad, I tap, and two days later a box arrives that I barely remember ordering.
I deleted all the shopping apps from my phone.
If I want something, I have to open the laptop and type it in deliberately.
That tiny friction saves me a fortune.
My grandmother used to say that money should be a little difficult to spend, so you respect it.
Your grandmother sounds like she understood everything we're talking about today.
She kept every receipt in a shoebox and balanced her checkbook by hand.
Seeing your spending written down is powerful.
Numbers on a screen don't feel real.
One more confession: I once bought the same pair of boots twice because I forgot I'd ordered them.
I gave one pair to my sister.
She still brings it up at every family dinner.
You know, most people don't lose money in one dramatic moment.
They squander it slowly, a forgotten subscription at a time.
Now let me ask you something.
What's the single best money decision you've ever made?
Setting up automatic transfers to savings on payday.
I never see the money, so I never miss it.
It just quietly grows in the background.
Pay yourself first, before anyone else gets a cent.
Learning to cook properly in my twenties.
It paid for itself a thousand times over.
Every meal I make at home is money that stays in my pocket.
All those kitchen gadgets I bought and never used.
Is there any way to recoup that money?
You won't recoup the full amount, but you'll recoup more than you'd expect.
I listed the espresso machine yesterday.
If it sells, I'll recoup about half of what I paid.
That's real money back in your pocket.
And it clears physical space too, which has its own value.
Do you ever feel that being this careful makes life less fun?
But then I remember that money stress is the least fun thing of all.
I'd rather be frugal and calm than flashy and anxious.
You know what surprised me, though?
Growing up around affluent families taught me that wealthy people negotiate constantly.
The most affluent person I know argues over hotel bills.
Wealthy people stay wealthy partly because they question every charge.
My old boss was a millionaire, and he'd spend twenty minutes disputing a forty-dollar fee.
He refused to let anyone squander his money, including himself.
People assume the rich just squander money left and right, but the ones who keep it are usually disciplined.
So what's the difference between frugal and thrifty?
I'd say frugal describes your attitude, choosing to spend less.
Thrifty describes your methods, the clever tactics you use.
So a frugal person skips the expensive coffee shop, and a thrifty person finds excellent beans on sale and brews at home.
You can be one without the other, but they're a powerful combination.
My goal for next year: less lavish impulse buying, more careful planning.
And the next time I get an unexpected bonus, I'm saving half before I even celebrate.
And if a boutique tries to charge you a crazy markup, you'll walk straight to the market and haggle like your grandmother.
Maybe I'll even teach you to loosen up a little, and you can teach me to tighten up.
Before we wrap up, let's do a lightning round.
Mine: wait forty-eight hours before any unplanned purchase.
Mine: audit your subscriptions twice a year.
You'll be shocked at what you're still paying for.
And one more from me: learn the difference between price and value.
Something cheap that breaks in a month is no bargain.
And from me: celebrate the small wins.
Every time you resist an impulse buy, that's a victory worth noticing.
Thanks for joining us on Word Kitchen.
Use these words this week, in real conversations, and notice how much richer your English becomes.
Remember, your money should work as hard as you do.
